title: How much drinking water to plan for
also: how much water do I need
def: Plan on at least one gallon (about 4 liters) of drinking water per person per day for emergencies, and more in heat, with illness, or for children and nursing mothers.
look: pale yellow urine means you are drinking enough
dark urine, dry mouth, headache, and dizziness mean you need more
very little urine for many hours is dangerous
use: Store at least three days of water for each person at home. In the field, carry what you need for the day plus a way to treat more, and sip steadily.
not: Do not ration water by waiting until you are thirsty; do not drink too much plain water all at once.
call: Call 911 for confusion, fainting, or no urination for many hours.

title: Is this water safe to drink?
also: can I drink from the stream
def: Clear water from a stream, lake, or spring can still carry germs, so treat it unless you know it is safe; clear does not mean clean.
look: clear but untreated water can hold Giardia, Cryptosporidium, bacteria, and viruses
fuel, chemical, or flood water is not made safe by boiling
dead animals, farms, and campsites upstream raise the risk
use: Treat all wild water before drinking: boil, use a filter, or use a disinfectant, and strain cloudy water first. Choose the clearest, moving source.
not: Do not drink from radiator or boiler water, seawater, or urine, and do not trust clear water on sight.
call: Get care for severe diarrhea, vomiting, or fever after drinking untreated water.

title: How to boil water
also: boil water to make it safe
def: Boiling is the most reliable way to kill germs: bring water to a rolling boil for one minute, or three minutes above 6,500 feet (2,000 m).
look: large bubbles breaking the surface
settle or strain cloudy water first
let it cool in the covered pot
use: Strain cloudy water through a clean cloth or coffee filter, bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 feet), let it cool, and store it in a clean, covered container.
not: Do not use boiling to make fuel, chemical, or seawater safe; it will not remove them.
steps: Strain cloudy water through a clean cloth or coffee filter.
Bring it to a rolling boil.
Hold the boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 6,500 feet.
Cool it covered and pour into a clean container.
call: Use a boil-water notice from your health department as the rule when there is one.

title: Disinfecting water with household bleach
def: Plain unscented household bleach can disinfect clear water, but it works less well than boiling against Giardia and Cryptosporidium.
look: 8 drops of 6% bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25%), double for cloudy water
wait 30 minutes
a slight chlorine smell afterward
use: Strain cloudy water, add the right drops of regular unscented bleach (not scented, color-safe, or with additives) per gallon, stir, and wait 30 minutes. If there is no chlorine smell, repeat once and wait 15 minutes more.
not: Do not use scented, splash-less, or color-safe bleach. Do not use bleach as your only method when you can boil.
call: Call your health department if the water source may be contaminated by sewage or chemicals.

title: Portable water filters: what they remove
def: A portable filter strains out parasites and bacteria; most do not remove viruses or chemicals.
look: pore size about 1 micron or less stops Giardia and Cryptosporidium
0.3 micron or less also stops most bacteria
a filter rated as a purifier may handle viruses
use: Pre-filter cloudy water through cloth, then run it through the filter, and follow the maker's directions for cleaning. Disinfect or boil afterward if viruses or unknown sources are a concern.
not: Do not freeze a wet hollow-fiber filter, and do not assume a filter removes chemicals, fuel, or salt.

title: Filter first, then disinfect
def: Filtering removes parasites and bacteria and clears the water, and a disinfectant afterward handles viruses that pass through.
look: filter or settle first
then boil, or add bleach or a chlorine dioxide tablet
wait the full contact time
use: When you are in doubt or in a place with viruses of concern, filter first and then disinfect the filtered water. This also saves disinfectant and gives it more reliable contact.
not: Do not use a disinfectant on very cloudy water without filtering first.

title: Cloudy water: settle or pre-filter
def: Cloudy water hides germs from disinfectant and clogs filters, so let it settle and strain it first.
look: silt or particles in the water
a clean cloth or coffee filter
a settled layer at the bottom
use: Let the water sit until the silt sinks, pour the clear top through a clean cloth or coffee filter, then boil, filter, or disinfect.
not: Do not skip the pre-filter and just add more disinfectant.

title: Water that cannot be made safe in the field
def: Water contaminated with fuel, chemicals, sewage, or flood debris cannot be made safe by boiling or bleach, so do not use it to drink.
look: an oily sheen or fuel smell
flood water with sewage or farm runoff
water near an industrial spill or a dead animal
use: Find another source, use bottled water, or follow your local health department's instructions. Use contaminated water only for flushing or cleaning, not for drinking or washing dishes.
not: Do not drink it, brush teeth with it, or use it for baby formula.
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 if someone swallowed it.

title: Containers and storing treated water
also: what to use for a water bottle
def: Store treated water in clean, food-grade containers with tight lids, away from sun and heat.
look: food-grade plastic or stainless steel
a lid that seals
a cool, dark place
use: Wash containers with soap and rinse, fill with treated water, label them with the date, and replace commercial water as the package says. In the field, use a pot, a bottle, or a clean bag.
not: Do not use a container that held chemicals, fuel, or milk.

title: Finding water in New England woods
also: where to find water in the woods
def: In New England, water is usually near: look for streams in valley bottoms, springs, ponds, and melted snow; moving water is better than still.
look: valley bottoms and seeps where several slopes meet
springs and clear running streams
packed snow and ice, melted first
use: Follow downhill and listen for running water, collect from the clearest moving source, and treat it. Melt snow or ice in a pot; do not eat it raw.
not: Do not drink from radiators, boilers, seawater, or urine, and do not eat snow to get water because it lowers your body temperature.
region: Beaver ponds, farm fields, and campsites upstream are common contamination sources in New England; Giardia is widespread in surface water.

title: Melting snow and ice for water
def: Melt snow or ice in a pot and treat the water; eating snow lowers body temperature and uses energy.
look: a pot with a little water in it to start
clean white snow, not yellow or near a road
ice yields more water than fluffy snow
use: Start with a little water in the pot so it doesn't scorch, add snow gradually, and boil it. Melt it with a stove or fire, or in a bag against the body only if needed.
not: Do not eat large amounts of snow in the cold.

title: Collecting rain
def: Rain is a good source if you collect it in clean containers, and you should treat it if it passed over roofs or leaves.
look: a tarp funneling water into a clean pot
rain caught directly is cleaner
roof runoff can have debris
use: Set clean containers out, rig a tarp to funnel rain into them, and let the first few minutes of rain wash dust off. Treat the water if it is for drinking.
not: Do not drink water from a roof treated with chemicals or stored in dirty containers.

title: Giardia and Cryptosporidium
def: Giardia and Cryptosporidium are tiny parasites in surface water that cause days of diarrhea, cramps, and nausea; boiling or the right filter stops them.
look: watery diarrhea, gas, cramps, and nausea one to two weeks after drinking
found in streams, lakes, and ponds, even clear ones
chlorine alone works poorly on Cryptosporidium
use: Boil water or use a filter rated for 1 micron or smaller. Wash your hands with soap and clean water before eating.
not: Do not rely on bleach alone for Cryptosporidium.
call: Get care for diarrhea that lasts more than a few days, or with fever, blood, or dehydration.

title: Iodine and chlorine dioxide tablets
def: Tablets disinfect water when boiling is not possible; follow the label for dose and wait time.
look: chlorine dioxide tablets kill most germs including Cryptosporidium after the label wait time
iodine tablets are less reliable against Cryptosporidium
taste and color changes
use: Read the label, pre-filter cloudy water, add the tablet, and wait the full time (often 30 minutes to 4 hours for Cryptosporidium).
not: Do not use iodine for pregnant women, people with thyroid problems, or long-term use.

title: UV purifiers and solar disinfection
def: UV treatment works only on clear water in a working unit, and solar disinfection needs clear plastic bottles in strong sun for many hours.
look: clear, not cloudy, water
a charged, working UV unit
clear PET bottles in full sun for 6 hours or two days in cloudy weather
use: Pre-filter, treat with the UV unit as directed, and carry a backup like tablets or a pot. Use solar disinfection only as a last resort.
not: Do not trust UV in cloudy water or with low batteries.

title: Washing hands, dishes, and wounds when water is scarce
def: When water is short, use the cleanest water for drinking and wound care, and a little soap and treated water for hands.
look: a small amount of soap and water for hands
alcohol-based sanitizer when hands are not greasy
dishes washed away from streams
use: Wash hands before eating and after the toilet, use treated water for wounds, and use hand sanitizer if there is no water. Wash dishes well away from streams.
not: Do not use contaminated water on wounds.

title: Latrine placement away from water
also: where to go to the bathroom outdoors
def: Dig a latrine or cathole at least 200 feet (60 m) from water, trails, and camp to keep your drinking water clean.
look: a hole 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) deep
200 feet from any stream, pond, or spring
downhill and downstream from camp
use: Dig a small hole, use it, cover it with soil, and wash your hands. Pack out toilet paper if the rules require it.
not: Do not go near water, and do not use areas near a drainage.

title: Baby formula when tap water is unsafe
def: Mix infant formula with bottled, boiled-and-cooled, or properly treated water when the tap is unsafe.
look: a boil-water notice or a flood
bottled water for babies
ready-to-feed formula needs no water
use: Use bottled or boiled water (cooled to room temperature before mixing, per the label), wash bottles with safe water, and use ready-to-feed formula if you can.
not: Do not use untreated or contaminated water, and do not dilute formula to stretch it.
call: Call a pediatrician or 911 if a baby is vomiting, lethargic, or not feeding.

title: Water sources never to drink
def: Never drink radiator or boiler water, seawater, urine, or water that has fuel or chemicals in it.
look: antifreeze in radiators
salt in seawater and urine
chemicals in pool or flood water
use: Use another source; if you must use pool water, treat and filter it, and use a toilet tank only if it is clean, not a bowl.
not: Do not drink seawater or urine; the salt makes you more dehydrated.
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 if anyone drinks antifreeze or chemical water.

title: Well disinfection after a flood
def: A flooded well must be tested and disinfected following health-department or EPA directions; do not invent a mix.
look: flood water over the wellhead
cloudy or odd-tasting water
a pump that was underwater
use: Use bottled or boiled water until the well is tested and cleared. Contact your health department or a certified lab, and follow their disinfection steps.
not: Do not drink or cook with the water until it is tested.
